statements.quote: Here is a tension worth sitting with.

statements.quote: An RNN keeps its state in a single hidden vector that it updates one token at a time, carrying everything forward.

statements.quote: A transformer has **no such carried-over hidden vector**: within a single forward pass it is a *parallel* function applied to the whole context at once, with no step-by-step evolution.

statements.quote: You are right that "time" barely exists for the network inside one forward pass — the only real notion of order is the **sequence position** of the tokens (and, during generation, the autoregressive step-by-step decoding).

statements.quote: Given that, the puzzle is sharper, not softer: how can a network with no carried-over memory do anything *sequential* or *stateful* — parse a sentence, follow a procedure, track a running count — when it has nowhere to keep the running total?

statements.quote: The reframe is that the state is **not absent, it is distributed**.

statements.quote: The "state" is the **residual stream plus the Key/Value vectors of every past token**.
statements.section: A Transformer as a State Machine: How a Stateless Network Keeps State

blocks.quote: Two Lessons in One
blocks.section: Two Lessons in One

blocks.quote: This chapter has two halves. The first asks a question that took two thousand years to be *asked*: **what makes a procedure an *algorithm*?** — and follows the answer through Euclid's gcd, the Sieve of Eratosthenes, and the 1928 decision problem that forced the entire theory of computation to be invented. The second shows a modern transformer *executing* algorithms on its own: grokking the Discrete Fourier Transform without being told it, and running code that exists only in the prompt. Read the first half to understand the object being executed; the second is the machine that runs it.
blocks.section: Two Lessons in One

blocks.quote: You have used the word *algorithm* so many times it has lost all meaning. A sorting step is an algorithm. A search is an algorithm. The way your coffee machine cycles through its modes is, in the strict sense, an algorithm. But there is a question almost nobody asks, and it is the one this whole field was eventually built around: **what makes a procedure an *algorithm* — as opposed to just a set of steps you happen to run?**
blocks.section: Two Lessons in One

blocks.quote: Two properties, and they are the entire game.
blocks.section: Two Lessons in One

blocks.quote: A procedure that has both is an algorithm. The rest of this half is the story of those two properties — and of how, in a single decade, they went from being quietly *practiced* for two thousand years to being rigorously *studied*.
blocks.section: Two Lessons in One

blocks.quote: Euclid's algorithm (c. 300 BC): the first with a surviving proof
blocks.section: Euclid's algorithm (c. 300 BC): the first with a surviving proof

blocks.quote: One of the oldest algorithms still in use every day sits in Euclid's *Elements*, Book VII (\cite[Euclidean algorithm]{euclideanalgorithm}; \cite[The Elements]{euclidelements}); Babylonian scribes were already writing step-by-step procedures a millennium and a half earlier (\cite[Knuth, 1972]{knuth1972babylonian}). Given two whole numbers, find their **greatest common divisor** — the largest number that divides both. The procedure:
blocks.section: Euclid's algorithm (c. 300 BC): the first with a surviving proof

blocks.quote: > Divide the larger by the smaller. Replace the pair by *(the smaller, the remainder)*. Repeat until the remainder is zero. The last non-zero remainder is the answer.
blocks.section: Euclid's algorithm (c. 300 BC): the first with a surviving proof

blocks.quote: It is an algorithm in the full, strong sense — and the *why* is the point, because it is the earliest example we have of someone *checking the two properties*.
blocks.section: Euclid's algorithm (c. 300 BC): the first with a surviving proof

blocks.quote: For the next two thousand years, this was just *the way you found a common divisor*. Nobody wrote "this procedure provably terminates and is provably correct," because the idea of checking those two things **in general** had not yet occurred to anyone.
blocks.section: Euclid's algorithm (c. 300 BC): the first with a surviving proof

blocks.quote: Watch it terminate Pick two positive integers and run the algorithm. Watch the middle column shrink — that shrinking is the *proof* the process has to stop.

blocks.quote: The gap: two thousand years of *doing*, none of *studying*
blocks.section: The gap: two thousand years of *doing*, none of *studying*

blocks.quote: Here is the gap the rest of the course has been circling. For all that, the algorithm was never a **thing**. It was a **verb**. People *did* algorithms; no one *studied* them as objects with properties you could check.
blocks.section: The gap: two thousand years of *doing*, none of *studying*

blocks.quote: The name is itself a fossil of that gap. *Algorithm* is the Latinized form of the name of the Persian mathematician al-Khwarizmi, whose ninth-century arithmetic gave us the word \cite[the etymology of "algorithm" (Wikipedia)]{historyofmath_wikipedia} — the course traces al-Khwarizmi himself in [The Brief History of AI](history.php). But al-Khwarizmi *named and catalogued* procedures — he did not ask the question that actually matters, and that nobody had asked before:
blocks.section: The gap: two thousand years of *doing*, none of *studying*

blocks.quote: > Is there a **general, universal** procedure? Can one machine, running one rule, decide the answer to *any* problem in a class — not just *this* gcd, or *this* sieve, but *any* instance, for all time?
blocks.section: The gap: two thousand years of *doing*, none of *studying*

blocks.quote: Naming a class of things is not the same as asking whether the class has a single procedure that handles all of it. That question — and it is *the* question — sat unasked until the twentieth century.
blocks.section: The gap: two thousand years of *doing*, none of *studying*

blocks.quote: Al-Khwarizmi's *al-Kitab al-jabr* (c. 820) is the bridge between the Babylonian recipe and the modern algorithm: it states a general procedure for solving quadratics and then demonstrates it on every case, with a geometric proof for each. The Latin translation of his name became *algorismus*, the medieval name for the Hindu-Arabic calculation method, and eventually "algorithm" (\cite[al-Khwarizmi, c. 820]{alkhwarizmi820algebra}; \cite[history of mathematics]{historyofmath_wikipedia}). What he still lacked was the question of whether one procedure could decide an entire class of problems -- the question Hilbert would pose in 1928.
blocks.section: The gap: two thousand years of *doing*, none of *studying*

blocks.quote: The question that built everything: the Entscheidungsproblem (1928)
blocks.section: The question that built everything: the Entscheidungsproblem (1928)

blocks.quote: In 1928 the mathematician David Hilbert (\cite[Hilbert & Ackermann, 1928]{hilbert1928entscheidung}) posed a question that had been waiting, unasked, for two thousand years. In German it is the **Entscheidungsproblem**, the decision problem:
blocks.section: The question that built everything: the Entscheidungsproblem (1928)

blocks.quote: > Given any statement of arithmetic — or, more generally, any formula of logic — does there exist a **general, mechanical procedure** that decides, in a finite number of steps, whether the statement is provable?
blocks.section: The question that built everything: the Entscheidungsproblem (1928)

blocks.quote: This is exactly the question Euclid's two properties had been pointing at all along. An *algorithm* was, quietly, a candidate *answer*: a mechanical procedure that terminates and is correct. The Entscheidungsproblem asks whether such a procedure exists **in general** — not for this problem, but for the whole class. Hilbert was confident the answer was **yes**; he was actively looking for the procedure.
blocks.section: The question that built everything: the Entscheidungsproblem (1928)

blocks.quote: The answer, delivered eight years later by two independent mathematicians wielding two tools that looked nothing alike, was **no**.
blocks.section: The question that built everything: the Entscheidungsproblem (1928)

blocks.quote: \marginfig{hilbert_1907.jpg}{David Hilbert (1862–1943), 1907. Public domain.}
blocks.section: The question that built everything: the Entscheidungsproblem (1928)

blocks.quote: 1936: two machines, one answer
blocks.section: 1936: two machines, one answer

blocks.quote: Kurt Gödel had already delivered the first blow in 1931 with his incompleteness theorems \cite[Gödel's incompleteness theorems (1931)]{godel1931incompleteness}: no consistent, effectively axiomatized system that can express basic arithmetic can prove every true statement in it. But incompleteness left a door open — it says some truths escape *proof*, not that no *procedure* could still decide which statements are decidable. The decision problem was still, as far as anyone could tell, on the table.
blocks.section: 1936: two machines, one answer

blocks.quote: In 1936, working independently, **Alonzo Church** and **Alan Turing** each wrote down a rigorous formalism for "mechanical procedure," and each used it to answer the 1928 question with a proof that the answer is **no** \cite[The Church–Turing Thesis (SEP)]{churchturing1936}. Turing learned of Church's result while his own paper was in press, and added an appendix proving the two formalisms equivalent.
blocks.section: 1936: two machines, one answer

blocks.quote: The two formalisms look nothing alike. One is a calculus; the other is a physical picture of a head on a tape. And yet they compute *exactly* the same set of functions — every problem one can solve, the other can solve too. That coincidence is so load-bearing that it has its own name: the \cite[Church–Turing thesis (SEP)]{churchturing1936}.
blocks.section: 1936: two machines, one answer

blocks.quote: And the upshot for the 1928 question: within this shared class of "what a machine can do," the validity of a first-order formula is not decidable in general. The Entscheidungsproblem has *no solution* — not because no one was clever enough to find the procedure, but because the procedure is provably *not there*. The question itself has no "yes."
blocks.section: 1936: two machines, one answer

blocks.quote: That is the "displaced prerequisite" this first half is filling. Everything in the second half of this chapter, and in [Software](software.php) — the idea that a computation has a *cost*, a *guarantee*, and a *limit* — rests on the fact that, in 1936, the algorithm stopped being a verb and became a noun. You can now hold one in your hand and take it apart: ask whether it stops, prove whether it is right, and measure how much work it does. Euclid had the algorithm. Hilbert asked the question. Church and Turing built the machine that *is* the answer.
blocks.section: The payoff: the algorithm becomes an object

blocks.quote: > A procedure becomes an **algorithm** when two things hold: it **terminates** for every input it promises to handle, and it is **correct by construction**. The question "is there a *general* procedure?" — the Entscheidungsproblem, 1928 — is what turned that property from a verb into an object, and forced the entire theory of computation to be built.
blocks.section: The payoff: the algorithm becomes an object

blocks.quote: What an algorithm costs
blocks.section: What an algorithm costs

blocks.quote: The mid-twentieth century made algorithms into engineering objects. Binary search -- repeatedly halving a sorted interval -- was described by John Mauchly in 1946 and analyzed in the early 1960s; Knuth's *Sorting and Searching* gave its exact comparison count and a canonical correct formulation (\cite[Binary search]{binarysearch_wiki}; \cite[Knuth]{taocp3}). Dijkstra's 1968 letter against the `goto` statement argued that programs should be built from structured control flow so their progress can be reasoned about, and Hoare's 1969 axioms gave a formal logic for assignments and while-loops -- the beginning of program verification (\cite[Dijkstra, 1968]{dijkstra1968goto}; \cite[Hoare, 1969]{hoare1969axiomatic}).
blocks.section: What an algorithm costs

blocks.quote: Two questions turned algorithms into a mathematical theory. Cook (1971) and Levin (1973) showed that a single problem -- Boolean satisfiability -- is complete for the class NP: if it had a polynomial-time algorithm, so would every problem whose solution can be checked in polynomial time (\cite[Cook, 1971]{cook1971complexity}; \cite[Cook-Levin theorem]{cooklevin_wiki}). Bellman's *Dynamic Programming* (1957) gave the complementary positive technique: break a problem into overlapping subproblems, store each answer once, and build the optimum from optimal subproblems (\cite[Bellman, 1957]{bellman1957book}). Together they defined the modern question -- not just can it be computed, but at what cost.
blocks.section: What an algorithm costs

blocks.quote: Modern algorithms increasingly search rather than calculate. PageRank (1998) treated the web as a Markov chain and ranked pages by the stationary distribution of a random surfer, turning a graph into a single global importance score (\cite[Brin & Page, 1998]{brin1998pagerank}). AlphaGo (2016) combined a policy network, a value network, and Monte Carlo tree search to beat Lee Sedol at Go -- a game whose branching factor had defeated pure search (\cite[Silver et al., 2016]{silver2016go}). Both are algorithms in the old sense -- they terminate and are correct relative to a model -- but their guarantee is statistical or empirical, not a proof of optimality.
blocks.section: What an algorithm costs

blocks.quote: Beyond modular arithmetic

blocks.quote: Beyond Modular Arithmetic: Magnitude, Comparison, and Counting
blocks.section: Beyond Modular Arithmetic: Magnitude, Comparison, and Counting

blocks.quote: The circular representations above solve a very specific problem: **modular** addition, where the answer wraps around a fixed modulus ($\bmod N$). That is a *bounded, cyclic* task — there is no "carry out to infinity," and no question of how *big* a number is. Once you leave that world, the model hits two different walls, and understanding them clarifies what a "number" actually is inside the network.
blocks.section: Beyond Modular Arithmetic: Magnitude, Comparison, and Counting

blocks.quote: Where does this live? In the **hidden states (the residual stream) of the later layers**, not in the input embedding. The circular probes decode the digits reliably from about the **third layer onward** (the first couple of layers are still busy "contextualizing" a multi-digit number, whose several tokens have to be combined first), and a causal intervention that rotates one digit's angle by $+5 \bmod 10$ modifies that digit in the model's answer — the exact intended result appears in only about 10–15% of cases (roughly half are "close"), so the code is genuinely *used*, not merely readable. (The paper's honest caveat: this is one strong, causally-active representation; it may be one of several redundant ones packed in superposition, not the only numeracy signal.) The tell-tale signature is the *error pattern*: arithmetic mistakes cluster on a **single digit** of the answer (the model emits "633" or "823" instead of "833"), exactly what a digit-wise code predicts — not the value-adjacent slips ("831", "834") a real number-line representation would produce. There is no clean, monotonic magnitude to "read off" and compare, which is why comparing small numbers is so error-prone: the model holds a digit-by-digit code, not a quantity.
blocks.section: Beyond Modular Arithmetic: Magnitude, Comparison, and Counting

blocks.quote: \cite[Cacioli (2026)]{cacioli2026weber} brought the formal tools of psychophysics to the question. First, **Weber's law** — a 19th-century finding about human perception: the smallest difference you can notice between two stimuli is a constant *fraction* of their size, not a constant *amount*. You tell 10 from 11 instantly, but not 1000 from 1001, because the gap (1) shrinks relative to the magnitude. The consequence is that magnitudes are spaced **logarithmically** in perception: a fixed *ratio* (×1.1) is a fixed *distance*, whether you are near 10 or near 1000. (\cite[Cacioli, 2026]{cacioli2026weber}) found the transformer's magnitude geometry has exactly this **log-compressive, Weber-law** structure (a 10% step is a constant distance), which also resolves a live disagreement in the literature (linear spacing? log? per-digit?). But the decisive finding is a **dissociation**: a model can *have* this logarithmic magnitude geometry and *still* perform at chance on discrimination tasks. Representing magnitude and being *able to use it to compare* are not the same thing — the geometry is necessary but not sufficient.
blocks.section: Beyond Modular Arithmetic: Magnitude, Comparison, and Counting

blocks.quote: A Transformer as a State Machine: How a Stateless Network Keeps State
blocks.section: A Transformer as a State Machine: How a Stateless Network Keeps State

blocks.quote: Here is a tension worth sitting with. An RNN keeps its state in a single hidden vector that it updates one token at a time, carrying everything forward. A transformer has **no such carried-over hidden vector**: within a single forward pass it is a *parallel* function applied to the whole context at once, with no step-by-step evolution. You are right that "time" barely exists for the network inside one forward pass — the only real notion of order is the **sequence position** of the tokens (and, during generation, the autoregressive step-by-step decoding). So "state across time" below means **state across the token positions / decode steps**, not an internal clock. Given that, the puzzle is sharper, not softer: how can a network with no carried-over memory do anything *sequential* or *stateful* — parse a sentence, follow a procedure, track a running count — when it has nowhere to keep the running total?
blocks.section: A Transformer as a State Machine: How a Stateless Network Keeps State

blocks.quote: The reframe is that the state is **not absent, it is distributed**. The "state" is the **residual stream plus the Key/Value vectors of every past token**. Each past token's hidden state is a register that the current token can read from through attention, and each new token writes a fresh entry. The whole sequence is, in effect, a **work tape / register file** that the model re-reads every step. (\cite[Katharopoulos et al., 2020]{katharopoulos2020linear}) made the relationship to recurrence literal: a *linear*-attention transformer has an exact **iterative (RNN-like) implementation**, where a single accumulated matrix plays the role of the hidden state. "Stateless" is therefore a misnomer; the state is just stored *in the context* rather than in a vector.
blocks.section: A Transformer as a State Machine: How a Stateless Network Keeps State

blocks.quote: Formally, this is enough to run a state machine. A single attention layer can implement the transitions of a **finite-state automaton** — softly, through the softmax, or exactly under a hardmax. (\cite[Adriaensen & Maene, 2024]{adriaensen2024moore}) took this concretely: they trained transformers on regular languages and then **extracted the finite-state (Moore) machine the network had implicitly built**, using queries and counterexamples rather than reading the states out of the weights. You can pull the state machine *out* of the transformer.
blocks.section: A Transformer as a State Machine: How a Stateless Network Keeps State

blocks.quote: But the power is bounded, and (\cite[Hahn, 2020]{hahn2020limitations}) pins down where. Because the context length is fixed, the number of distinct "states" a single forward pass can hold is finite — a fixed-size, fixed-context transformer is a **finite-state machine**, and it cannot model periodic or truly hierarchical languages unless its depth or head-count scales with the input. The mechanistic engine behind the sequential behavior is the **induction head** (\cite[Olsson et al., 2022]{olsson2022induction}) — find $[A][B]\ldots[A]$, copy the successor $[B]$ — which is a primitive form of **recurrence** (copy what followed a repeated pattern). And (\cite[von Oswald et al., 2022]{vonoswald2022indc}) read the whole forward pass as **in-context gradient descent**, with the residual stream holding an *evolving in-context model*. So "recurrence" in a transformer is not a stored hidden vector being updated; it is attention **re-reading an ever-growing store of past states** and refining them layer by layer, a hand-off between specialized heads in successive layers that is carried by thin low-rank "channels" in the residual stream (\cite[Merullo et al., 2024]{merullo2024talkingheads}).
blocks.section: A Transformer as a State Machine: How a Stateless Network Keeps State

blocks.quote: The honest summary: a transformer performs sequential, stateful computation by treating the context itself as state — a soft state machine whose state space is bounded by its (fixed) depth and context window. That bound is precisely what limits the arithmetic and counting of the previous section, and the binding limits you meet in the fact-retrieval chapter.
blocks.section: A Transformer as a State Machine: How a Stateless Network Keeps State
